rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all eight compounds and locate the elution window and critical pairs. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. The short elution window leaves ample room for subsequent gradient refinement.

Halve the gradient slope at the better-performing temperature to test whether the remaining close pairs separate as the elution window expands. The previous last peak at 5.08 minutes provides room for this slower gradient before the time penalty becomes significant.

Further reduce the gradient slope to improve the sole remaining critical pair while preserving the resolved middle cluster. The last peak is expected near 10 minutes, offering a chance to reach full resolution without a time penalty.

The slower gradient drove the late critical pair toward coelution, so shorten the best gradient instead. An 18-minute gradient should improve that pair while testing whether the middle cluster retains sufficient resolution.

The best gradient is nearly fully resolved, but changing slope trades resolution between two critical pairs. Test a five-degree temperature decrease at that gradient to see whether selectivity can remove the remaining deficit.

Return to 60 °C and raise the starting organic fraction one step to adjust selectivity and slightly reduce the gradient slope. This tests another way to resolve the middle pair without sacrificing the nearby late pair.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 by narrowing the gradient range, aiming to lift both middle-pair resolutions above 1.5 while preserving the late pair’s margin. The final organic fraction remains above the composition at which all peaks previously eluted.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the marginal middle pairs above R = 1.5. The late critical pair should retain sufficient resolution, with all peaks eluting well before 10 minutes.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark while seeking a shorter fully resolved elution window. Raise the starting organic fraction and reduce the slope to compensate for the middle cluster’s sensitivity.

The higher starting organic fraction sacrificed middle-pair resolution, so retain injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark. Test the low-temperature endpoint with its gradient to explore a different selectivity regime that might permit a shorter fully resolved method.

Shorten the low-temperature gradient to test whether its sole critical pair improves with slope while reducing the last-peak time. Injection 9 remains the maximum-CRF benchmark if this alternative selectivity regime proves less effective.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 11’s slope to shorten the low-temperature elution window and test its effect on the critical pair. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Increase the starting organic fraction again at the same slope to test whether the critical pair separates after an elution-order reversal. This could yield a shorter fully resolved method; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one more step while preserving slope, following the improving critical-pair separation at 0.30. This tests whether full resolution can be achieved with an even shorter elution window.
Injection 15 achieves maximum CRF with a much shorter elution window. Shorten its gradient by one step to test whether the critical pairs retain R ≥ 1.5 as the last peak moves earlier.

Back off the slope by lowering the endpoint one grid step, placing it between the fully resolved injection 15 and the faster injection 16. This should restore the critical pair’s resolution while keeping the last peak earlier than in injection 15.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing critical-pair resolution. Retain injection 17 as the current shortest maximum-CRF benchmark.

Return to 25 °C and test a higher starting organic fraction at the same slope as injection 17, seeking a faster separation in a potentially different elution-order regime. Keep injection 17 as the shortest fully resolved benchmark.

Test a steeper gradient at 30 °C with a lower starting organic fraction to counter the middle-pair compression seen in injection 18. This seeks a shorter fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 17 as the benchmark.

Reduce injection 20’s slope to improve its sole unresolved pair while checking that the neighboring pair stays above R = 1.5. This targets full resolution near the four-minute elution window of injection 17.

Test whether warming the fast, high-starting-organic method separates its two critical pairs in this different elution-order regime. Injection 17 remains the shortest verified fully resolved method if this targeted temperature change fails.

Make the fast high-organic method substantially shallower to test whether its two marginal middle pairs can gain resolution with only a modest increase in elution time. Injection 17 remains the shortest verified maximum-CRF method.

Test an intermediate starting organic fraction with a shallow gradient to recover middle-pair resolution while exploiting earlier elution. Injection 17 remains the shortest verified fully resolved benchmark.

Shorten injection 24’s gradient one step to test how much of its resolution margin can be exchanged for earlier elution. The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 17 remaining the shortest verified fully resolved method.
